metadata.document: WHAT WHY HOW Exploring the fundamental questions for resource management law reform in Aotearoa New Zealand - Paper 1: Context

cleaned_body_text: Acknowledgements Grateful thanks go to the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society of New Zealand and the Michael and Suzanne Borrin Foundation for supporting this work. Thanks to those who have given up their time to be interviewed for the project and have reviewed this paper, and to members of the project’s advisory group, who provided valuable guidance and feedback. 1 Introduction “Reform is a treadmill.” The Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) is New Zealand’s primary environmental and planning law. It is responsible for controlling how land is used, as well as managing the impacts of activities on the environment (including freshwater, soil, air, the marine environment and biodiversity). The current coalition government, in ‘phase 3’ of its resource management reform programme, intends to replace the RMA with two separate acts. These are to be premised on the ‘enjoyment of property rights’. This reform follows close on the heels of the previous Labour government’s own replacements for the RMA (the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 (NBA) and Spatial Planning Act 2023 (SPA)), which lasted only a matter of months before being repealed (at which point the RMA was reinstated). Repealing these Acts was ‘phase 1’ of the current government’s reforms. A second phase involves two sets of amendments to the RMA, new and amended national direction, and the enactment of bespoke fast-track consenting legislation outside the RMA for nationally or regionally important projects (the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024). These ‘phase 2’ changes are proposed to be compatible with, and flow through into, the new framework under ‘phase 3’. The government has not yet made detailed policy decisions on ‘phase 3’. It has, however, provided a series of ten ‘design principles’ to guide it. It has also established an expert advisory panel (EAG) to provide advice on how to operationalise a new system based on its design principles. The EAG provided its report to Ministers at the end of 2024. At the time of writing, it has not been publicly released. Policy decisions on the major legislative architecture of the replacement RMA laws are to be taken by Cabinet in March 2025, and legislation is planned to be introduced in September 2025. The government’s ten principles guiding replacement laws for the RMA: Narrow the scope of the resource management system to focus on managing actual effects on the environment. Establish two Acts with clear and distinct purposes – one to manage environmental effects arising from activities, and another to enable urban development and infrastructure. Strengthen and clarify the role of environmental limits and how they are to be developed. Provide for greater use of national standards to reduce the need for resource consents and simplify council plans. Shift the focus away from consenting before activities can get underway, and towards compliance, monitoring and enforcement of activities’ compliance with national standards. Use spatial planning and a simplified designation process to lower the cost of future infrastructure. Realise efficiencies by requiring one regulatory plan per region, jointly prepared by regional and district councils. Provide for a rapid, low-cost resolution of disputes between neighbours and between property owners and councils, with the potential for a new Planning Tribunal (or equivalent). Uphold Treaty of Waitangi settlements and the Crown’s obligations. Provide faster and cheaper processes with less reliance on litigation, contained within shorter and simpler legislation that is more accessible. These ‘principles’ are a mix of relatively specific directions and a much more open-ended rethink. But they are all being guided by the broader idea that the system should be based on the enjoyment of property rights. Various speeches, and a high-level Cabinet paper, have provided some further insights into the government’s thinking about problems and solutions. In interviews we have conducted thus far, opposition political parties did not express specific views on ‘phase 3’ reforms, other than a degree of unease about a system premised on the enjoyment of property rights. However, interviewee representatives of Labour, Te Pati Māori and the Green Party all emphasised the importance of having meaningful environmental limits to constrain property rights, protecting the rights and interests of Māori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and building on the platform provided by policy work on the NBA and SPA. 2 The risks of flip-flopping “Every time … a potential change of government signals change, uncertainty reverberates through communities of land and water users, affecting their decisions.” Appetite for fundamental reform of the RMA has been growing for a decade, driven partly by poor environmental outcomes, decreased housing affordability, inconsistent implementation, and increasing cost and complexity of decision-making. However, a swinging cycle of repeal and enactment across governments will benefit no one, creating cost, instability, complexity and friction. There is a large fiscal cost in undertaking large policy and legislative processes, alongside significant transition costs including implementation and inevitable litigation costs. A microcosm of the impact of flip-flopping can be seen in the recent changes to the RMA that prevented the Otago Regional Council from notifying its freshwater plan, despite significant time and cost. Above all, flip flopping creates a risk to the natural environment. Environmental indicators can be eroded much faster than they can be restored. If a new system is to be durable, it needs to be developed through a process that is public facing and inclusive of different political and philosophical perspectives. 3 The EDS project The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) is conducting a project that seeks to go back to basics, examining what the core of a future resource management system should look like. The remainder of this paper provides the background to a series of papers that will explore three conceptual questions about the system: what is the resource management system, why does the system manage resources, and how should decisions be made. 4 Is RMA reform needed? No one should reform legislation for the sake of it, but the resource management system does need to change, and at its heart is the RMA. The RMA has failed to achieve the kinds of outcomes it was intended to achieve, including addressing social and economic challenges like housing affordability and enabling major infrastructure upgrades. Furthermore, the RMA has failed to achieve its primary goal of arresting the decline of the natural environment. Environmental reporting over the past decade reads as a litany of environmental loss, including depleted native forests, threatened species, lost wetlands, degraded waterways, and high greenhouse gas emissions. The second kind of problem with the RMA is procedural: it takes too long and costs too much money, is unpredictable and discretionary, has become increasingly complex and fragmented, is litigious, and fails to adequately involve Māori or align with other statutory frameworks. 5 Concluding comments and a word on property rights Any resource management framework reflects perspectives on what is right and wrong, and what ought to happen in response. Different worldviews approach the concept of property quite differently. At the heart of phase 3 reforms is the idea that property rights need to be respected and protected, but property rights are not absolute and have never been shielded from non-consensual regulatory controls. The fundamental logic for planning legislation is to constrain the exercise of property rights, thereby protecting the public interest and the natural environment.
